questions.title: Finger Thoracostomy
questions.stem: Which single finding must be present before a finger thoracostomy may be performed?
questions.explanation: Hypotension is stated in red as REQUIRED to perform a finger thoracostomy. Tachycardia, JVD and tracheal deviation are supporting signs of peri-arrest tension physiology, but none of them substitutes for hypotension as the trigger to cut.

questions.title: Finger Thoracostomy
questions.stem: Which condition is a contraindication to finger thoracostomy?
questions.explanation: Simple pneumothorax, normotension and hypertension are the listed contraindications — without tension physiology and hypotension there is nothing to decompress. Traumatic arrest is itself an indication, and decreased breath sounds and falling ETCO2 are supporting signs of tension.

questions.title: Finger Thoracostomy
questions.stem: Where is the incision placed for a finger thoracostomy?
options: 4th or 5th intercostal space, between the anterior and mid-axillary lines
2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
5th intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
4th or 5th intercostal space at the posterior axillary line
questions.explanation: The incision is lateral to the nipple at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, between the anterior and mid-axillary lines. The 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line is a needle thoracostomy site, not a finger thoracostomy site.

questions.title: Finger Thoracostomy
questions.stem: During a finger thoracostomy, if the provider is in doubt about which rib interspace to use, what is the advice?
options: Err one rib interspace more superior
Err one rib interspace more inferior
Default to the 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
Confirm the interspace with ultrasound before cutting
questions.explanation: When in doubt, err one interspace more superior. Going too low risks entering the abdomen through the diaphragm, which is a far worse error than opening the chest one space high.

questions.title: Finger Thoracostomy
questions.stem: During a finger thoracostomy, which instrument is used to pass through the soft tissue and enter the pleural space after the skin incision?
questions.explanation: The #10 scalpel makes the skin incision only; the large Kelly clamp, held by the shanks, is pushed through the soft tissue to the rib and then over its superior border into the pleural space. The Ruiz hook and bougie belong to the surgical cricothyrotomy kit.

questions.title: Finger Thoracostomy
questions.stem: During a finger thoracostomy, which structures lie at the inferior border of the rib and must be avoided?
options: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve
questions.explanation: The neurovascular bundle runs in the groove along the inferior rib border, so the clamp is pressed over the TOP of the rib. Striking that bundle causes brisk arterial bleeding into a chest that is already compromised.

questions.title: Finger Thoracostomy
questions.stem: During a finger thoracostomy, what is the next step immediately after the Kelly clamp has been pressed over the rib and into the pleural space?
options: Spread the clamp as you pull it out to enlarge the opening
Insert a gloved finger to verify entry into the pleura
Place a vented chest seal over the site
questions.explanation: The opening is enlarged by spreading the Kelly clamp as it is withdrawn, and only then is the gloved finger inserted to verify the pleura has been entered. Inserting the finger into an unspread tract usually fails to confirm anything.

questions.title: Finger Thoracostomy
questions.stem: During a finger thoracostomy, how is entry into the pleural space verified?
options: Insert a gloved finger and hook it against the inner side of the ribs
Auscultate for returning breath sounds on the treated side
Observe a rise in ETCO2 on the waveform
Look for a rush of air escaping the incision
questions.explanation: Confirmation is tactile: a gloved finger is inserted and hooked to feel the inner surface of the ribs. Rib fractures may be present and can lacerate the finger.

questions.title: Finger Thoracostomy
questions.stem: What estimated volume of blood return from a finger thoracostomy prompts an occlusive dressing and initiation of blood products?
questions.explanation: Excessive blood return estimated at more than 1000 mL means the open chest is now the exsanguination route, so the site is occluded deliberately to tamponade and blood products are started. The crew must then watch for a recurrent tension pneumothorax.

questions.title: Finger Thoracostomy
questions.stem: The patient re-tensions after a finger thoracostomy. What should the crew do?
options: Insert a finger into the existing incision
Make a new incision one interspace more superior
Perform a needle decompression on the same side
Place a vented chest seal over the incision
questions.explanation: The tract is already there; re-tensioning means it has sealed over, so the finger goes back into the existing incision to re-open the pleura. A second incision or a needle adds injury without addressing the closed tract.

questions.title: Flow-Safe II CPAP Delivery System
questions.stem: Which patient presentation is listed as an indication for the Flow-Safe II CPAP delivery system?
questions.explanation: CHF/pulmonary edema, asthma/COPD, moderate to severe respiratory distress and pre-oxygenation for RSI are the indications. Pneumothorax, frank respiratory failure and severe altered LOC are all contraindications — CPAP needs a patient who can breathe and protect the airway.

questions.title: Flow-Safe II CPAP Delivery System
questions.stem: Below what systolic blood pressure is the Flow-Safe II CPAP system contraindicated?
questions.explanation: SBP < 100 is a listed contraindication to Flow-Safe II CPAP. Positive intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return, so CPAP can tip a marginally compensated patient into frank hypotension.

questions.title: Flow-Safe II CPAP Delivery System
questions.stem: At or below what weight are pediatric patients contraindicated for the Flow-Safe II CPAP system, absent a ventilator malfunction?
questions.explanation: Pediatric patients weighing 15 kg or less are a contraindication unless the ventilator has malfunctioned. The Flow-Safe II is a fixed, flow-driven device with no ability to scale safely to a small child.

questions.title: Flow-Safe II CPAP Delivery System
questions.stem: On the Flow-Safe II flow chart, which oxygen flow rate corresponds to a desired PEEP of 10 cmH2O?
questions.explanation: The chart attached to the oxygen tubing pairs 5 cmH2O with 8–9 LPM, 7.5 cmH2O with 10–12 LPM, 10 cmH2O with 13–14 LPM, and 13 cmH2O (the maximum) with flush. The Flow-Safe II has no PEEP dial — flow IS the PEEP setting.

questions.title: Flow-Safe II CPAP Delivery System
questions.stem: By how much may the pressure shown on the Flow-Safe II manometer differ from the desired CPAP level?
questions.explanation: A reading within ± 3 cmH2O of the desired CPAP is acceptable. A larger discrepancy usually means a mask leak, which is corrected by repositioning or changing mask size rather than by turning up the flow.

questions.title: Flow-Safe II CPAP Delivery System
questions.stem: A patient requires both ventilatory and oxygenation support. What should be used instead of the Flow-Safe II CPAP device?
options: CPAP at a higher PEEP level
questions.explanation: The Flow-Safe II provides CPAP only, so it supports oxygenation but does nothing for ventilation. A patient who is also failing to ventilate needs BiPAP delivered through the transport ventilator.

questions.title: Flow-Safe II CPAP Delivery System
questions.stem: If nebulized medication is needed for a patient on the Flow-Safe II CPAP device, where is the nebulizer connected?
options: Between the mask and the Flow-Safe manometer via a T piece
Between the flow sensor and the ETT
Upstream of the device at the oxygen source
questions.explanation: The nebulizer set-up goes between the mask and the manometer using a T piece, so the drug is delivered close to the patient without disturbing the pressure reading. Its own oxygen tubing must run to a secondary oxygen source.

questions.title: Flow-Safe II CPAP Delivery System
questions.stem: When a nebulizer is added to the Flow-Safe II CPAP circuit, where is its oxygen tubing connected?
options: To the same oxygen source driving the CPAP
To a flow meter Christmas tree on the CPAP line
questions.explanation: The nebulizer runs off a second oxygen source. Sharing the CPAP source would steal flow and drop the delivered PEEP, which on this device is set purely by flow rate.

questions.title: Gastric Tube Insertion
questions.stem: Which patient condition is an indication for gastric tube insertion?
questions.explanation: Intubation, comatose patients, GI bleeds, overdoses, gastric distension and gastric obstruction are the indications. Esophageal rupture, caustic ingestion and severe facial trauma are contraindications — in each, blind tube passage risks creating or extending a perforation.

questions.title: Gastric Tube Insertion
questions.stem: A patient who needs gastric decompression has had recent nasal surgery. What should be done?
options: Place a nasogastric tube in the opposite nare
Place the nasogastric tube with extra lubrication
questions.explanation: Recent nasal surgery is a contraindication to the nasal route only — an OG may be placed instead. The other listed contraindications (esophageal rupture, caustic ingestion) rule out both routes.

questions.title: Gastric Tube Insertion
questions.stem: How is nasogastric tube insertion depth measured?
options: Tip of the nose to the corner of the ear, then to the xiphoid process
Corner of the mouth to the tip of the ear, then to the xiphoid process
Tip of the nose to the earlobe, then to the umbilicus
Corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw, then to the sternal notch
questions.explanation: The NG measurement starts at the tip of the nose; the mouth-to-ear-to-xiphoid route is the orogastric measurement. Using the OG measurement for an NG leaves the tube short of the stomach by roughly the length of the nasal passage.

questions.title: Gastric Tube Insertion
questions.stem: During nasogastric tube insertion the patient begins to cough and develops new onset dyspnea. What should be done?
options: Withdraw the tube slightly and reassess
Continue advancing as the patient swallows
questions.explanation: Coughing or new dyspnea suggests the tube has entered the airway, so the tube is removed rather than repositioned. Continuing to advance risks intubating the trachea with a gastric tube.

questions.title: Gastric Tube Insertion
questions.stem: What size syringe is used for aspirating gastric contents to assess gastric tube placement?
questions.explanation: A 60 mL syringe is connected and aspirated back while assessing for gastric contents. The same assessment then uses a separate injection of air while listening over the stomach.

questions.title: Gastric Tube Insertion
questions.stem: When confirming gastric tube placement, after aspirating for gastric contents, how much air is injected while listening over the stomach?
questions.explanation: Roughly 20 mL of air is injected and the crew listens or feels for the air rush in the stomach. This applies identically to the nasogastric and orogastric routes.

questions.title: Gastric Tube Insertion
questions.stem: Once gastric tube placement is confirmed, how should the tube be secured?
options: Tape it in place, but not to the ETT
Tape it to the ETT so the two move together
Suture it in place before transport
Secure it with a commercial tube holder
questions.explanation: The gastric tube should explicitly NOT be taped to the ETT. Tying the two together means any tug on the gastric tube transmits directly to the airway and risks extubation.

questions.title: Hemostatic Agents
questions.stem: Before packing a hemostatic agent into a wound, what should be done first?
options: Remove any saturated gauze from the wound
Irrigate the wound with sterile saline
Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound
Pack the wound with plain gauze first
questions.explanation: Saturated gauze is removed so the hemostatic agent can make direct contact with the bleeding vessels. An agent packed on top of blood-soaked gauze never reaches the source and will fail.

questions.title: Hemostatic Agents
questions.stem: After packing a hemostatic agent with rolled gauze into the wound, how long should direct pressure be held?
questions.explanation: A continuous 3 minutes of direct pressure is held on the bleeding source through the packed gauze. Releasing early is the most common reason a hemostatic dressing fails.

questions.title: Hemostatic Agents
questions.stem: A hemostatic dressing packed into a wound is now fully red. What should be done?
options: Remove it and replace it with a new hemostatic dressing
Add a second dressing on top and hold pressure
Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound
Wrap and tie the bandage to maintain pressure
questions.explanation: A fully red dressing means the agent was not applied to the bleeding source or pressure was not held long enough, so it is removed and replaced rather than layered over. Wrapping and tying is only done once bleeding is actually controlled.

questions.title: Hemostatic Agents
questions.stem: With which agent are QuickClot hemostatic dressings impregnated?
questions.explanation: QuickClot uses kaolin, an inorganic mineral. The dressings contain no human, animal or shellfish product and do not cause an exothermic reaction, so shellfish allergy and burn risk are not reasons to withhold them.

questions.title: Hemostatic Agents
questions.stem: How long may a hemostatic dressing remain in a wound?
questions.explanation: Dressings can stay packed for up to 24 hours, which comfortably covers any transport. There is no reason to disturb a controlled wound en route — 'if you peek, you leak.'

questions.title: Hemostatic Agents
questions.stem: Besides major hemorrhage, what other use for hemostatic agents is described?
options: Controlling nuisance bleeding such as head lacerations
Control of epistaxis after nasal airway placement
questions.explanation: Hemostatic agents are not reserved for exsanguinating injury — they are effective for persistent 'nuisance bleeding' such as scalp lacerations that would otherwise consume crew attention throughout transport.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: A patient is being prepared for RSI. What role does high flow nasal cannula play?
options: Pre-oxygenation and apneic oxygenation during RSI
A bridge to CPAP after extubation
questions.explanation: Pre and apneic oxygenation during RSI is an explicit indication — the high flow continues to drive oxygen into the airway through the apneic period. Hypoxia, hypercarbia and mild to moderate respiratory distress are the other listed indications.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: Which finding contraindicates high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: Basilar skull fracture is a contraindication because high flow into the nasopharynx can be driven through the skull base defect. Hypoxia, hypercarbia and mild to moderate distress are indications for the therapy.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: What is the adult flow rate range for high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: Adults are run at 8–60 LPM, titrated to work of breathing while FiO2 is titrated to oxygenation. The weight-based 0.5–1 L/kg/min figure is the pediatric rate, and the single-digit LPM figures belong to the Flow-Safe II CPAP chart.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: What is the pediatric flow rate range for high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: Pediatric HFNC starts at 0.5–1 L/kg/min. The 2 L/kg/min and 20 LPM figures are the ceiling that may be used only when transporting without heat and humidification, not the starting range.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: To what may pediatric high flow nasal cannula flow be titrated if there is no heat or humidification?
questions.explanation: Without heat and humidification the pediatric flow may be titrated up to 2 L/kg/min or 20 LPM. The 60 LPM ceiling applies to adults only.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: What is required before transporting an adult on high flow nasal cannula without heat and/or humidification?
options: Approval from the sending provider or OLMC
A physician escort for the transport
Notification of the receiving facility only
questions.explanation: This is carried in a red box: approval from the sending provider or OLMC is required for unheated, unhumidified HFNC in adults, because dry high flow gas rapidly dries secretions and injures the nasal mucosa.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: For high flow nasal cannula, how should the RAM cannula prongs be sized against the patient's nares?
options: They should not occlude more than 80% of the nares
They should completely occlude the nares to hold pressure
They should occlude roughly half of the nares
They should be sized to the smaller of the two nares
questions.explanation: The prongs must leave a leak — no more than 80% occlusion — so that exhaled gas can escape. A fully occlusive fit converts HFNC into an uncontrolled positive-pressure device.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: Which Hamilton T-1 mode is used for delivering high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: HFNC is run in HiFloO2 mode found under Noninvasive, with FiO2 and flow set independently. LPO is not available at all while HiFloO2 is running.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: A patient on high flow nasal cannula deteriorates during transport. What should the crew consider?
options: Increasing the flow rate above 60 LPM
Adding LPO mode to conserve oxygen
questions.explanation: HFNC has a ceiling; a deteriorating patient escalates to CPAP, BiPAP or RSI rather than to more flow. LPO is unavailable during HFNC therapy and a non-rebreather is a step down, not up.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: Which oxygen-conserving ventilator mode is unavailable while high flow nasal cannula therapy is running?
questions.explanation: LPO cannot be used during HFNC. If oxygen conservation becomes necessary on a long transport, the patient is switched to CPAP or BiPAP instead — which is why the LFN oxygen calculator must be run before departure.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: What is the therapeutic goal of high flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy?
options: Increase PaO2 to widen the oxygen diffusion gradient
Generate a set level of positive end-expiratory pressure
Unload the diaphragm to reduce work of breathing
Provide ventilatory as well as oxygenation support
questions.explanation: High flow delivers volumes beyond what the patient ventilates, washing out CO2 from the upper airway and raising delivered O2; the stated goal is a higher PaO2 and therefore a steeper diffusion gradient. It is not a pressure-targeted mode.

questions.title: High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.stem: If a Hamilton T-1 is not readily available for high flow nasal cannula, what alternative is permitted for the RAM cannula?
options: Regular oxygen tubing on a flow meter Christmas tree
A Flow-Safe II CPAP device with the mask removed
An LTV ventilator run in HiFloO2 mode
A non-rebreather reservoir line at 15 LPM
questions.explanation: The RAM cannula can be driven from regular oxygen tubing on a standard flow meter, but this gives a reduced maximum flow rate and no humidification.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: How many autofill cycles does the internal helium reservoir of the Maquet IABP hold?
questions.explanation: The internal reservoir carries enough helium for 36 autofill cycles. Because altitude change, power cycling and run time all consume cycles, the crew must budget them against the planned flight profile.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: How many autofill cycles does the Maquet IABP perform each time the pump is powered on or off, or the balloon is disconnected and reconnected?
questions.explanation: Each power cycle or balloon disconnect/reconnect costs 6 autofill cycles out of a reservoir of 36. Needless power cycling on the ramp can consume a third of the available helium before the flight begins.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: During IABP transport, at what interval of altitude GAIN does the Maquet pump perform an autofill cycle?
questions.explanation: An internal transducer senses barometric change, triggering one autofill for every 1000 feet of climb and one for every 2000 feet of descent. Climbing therefore burns helium twice as fast as descending.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: Apart from altitude change, at what interval does the Maquet IABP perform an additional autofill cycle?
questions.explanation: One extra autofill occurs for every 2 hours of pump operation. On a long fixed-wing leg this time-based consumption must be added to the altitude-driven cycles when estimating remaining helium.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: To what pressure should the IABP flush bag pressure infuser be inflated?
questions.explanation: The pressure bag is inflated to 300 mmHg, the line flushed for several seconds, and the zero button held for two seconds. Too little pressure allows blood to track back and damp or clot the inner lumen.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: The patient arrives on an Arrow pump with an Arrow fiber-optic balloon. What is required when transferring to the Maquet IABP console?
options: Use the pressure cable and transducer for the IAB
Zero the fiber-optic cable before pressing START
Connect the fiber-optic sensor cable first
Run the pump in semi-auto mode for the transport
questions.explanation: An Arrow fiber-optic balloon will not communicate with the Maquet console, so timing must come from the conventional pressure cable and transducer. Connecting the fiber-optic cable first applies only to a Maquet/Datascope balloon.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: The IABP arterial pressure waveform becomes damped in flight. What should be done first?
options: Aspirate 3 mL from the IAB inner lumen and discard it
Flush the inner lumen for 15 seconds
Place the pump on standby and switch to semi-auto
Cap the lumen and use an alternative pressure source
questions.explanation: Aspirating 3 mL first tells you whether the lumen is patent. If blood returns, the line is flushed for 15 seconds with the pump on standby; if nothing aspirates, the lumen is presumed clotted and is capped with an alternative pressure source used.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: How often should the IAB inner lumen be flushed during transport to prevent damping?
questions.explanation: A brief flush of the inner lumen every 15 minutes maintains patency. Losing the pressure waveform in flight costs the trigger source for timing if no fiber-optic cable is in place.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: Where should the IABP Augmentation alarm be set relative to the patient's augmented diastolic pressure?
questions.explanation: The augmentation alarm is set 10 mmHg below the patient's augmented diastolic pressure, roughly 3 minutes after assist begins. Set that close, any real loss of augmentation alarms promptly instead of being missed.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: Which operation mode is the default on the Maquet IABP?
questions.explanation: Auto is the default; semi-auto is rarely needed. In auto the pump selects the lead and trigger and manages inflation/deflation timing continuously, which is what you want in a vibrating, noisy aircraft.

questions.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (Maquet)
questions.stem: After the IABP and patient are loaded into the rotor-wing aircraft, where is the pump secured?
options: Between the stretcher and the aft-facing seat
Behind the forward-facing seat, left of the loading door
On the brownline rail with the foam pad removed
At the forward bulkhead beside the patient's head
questions.explanation: In the rotor the IABP sits between the stretcher and the aft-facing seat; behind the forward-facing seat left of the patient loading door is the fixed-wing position. In both, the foam pad keeps the pump off the brownline rail and Pilatus tie-down straps run through the pump handles.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Which airway reflex finding is required before an i-gel is placed?
questions.explanation: The indication is an unconscious patient with respiratory compromise AND an absent gag reflex; a responsive patient with a gag reflex is an explicit contraindication, since the device will be rejected or provoke vomiting.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Which condition is a contraindication to the i-gel?
questions.explanation: Known esophageal disease, caustic ingestion and a responsive patient with a gag reflex are the contraindications. Unconsciousness, respiratory compromise and an absent gag reflex together form the indication.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Which i-gel size is indicated for a 70 kg adult?
questions.explanation: Size 4 (green) is the medium adult device covering 50–90 kg. Size 3 is the small adult at 30–60 kg and size 5 the large adult at 90+ kg, so a 70 kg patient falls squarely in size 4.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: What type of lubricant is used for the i-gel?
questions.explanation: A small bolus of water-based lubricant is used on the back, sides and front of the cuff; silicone-based lubricants are explicitly prohibited. No bolus may be left sitting in the bowl of the cuff, where it would be driven into the airway on insertion.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: When placing an i-gel, how should the patient's head and neck be positioned, trauma permitting?
options: Sniffing position, head extended and neck flexed
Neutral in-line with a chin lift
Full extension with the shoulders padded
Supine with support under the shoulders and neck
questions.explanation: The sniffing position with head extended and neck flexed aligns the hypopharynx for the device to glide along the hard palate. The chin is gently pressed down before insertion begins.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: When placing an i-gel, in which direction is the leading soft tip introduced into the mouth?
options: Toward the floor of the mouth
questions.explanation: The tip is introduced toward the hard palate, then glided downward and backward along it with continuous gentle pressure until definitive resistance is felt. Aiming elsewhere tends to fold the tip or catch the tongue.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: Early resistance is met during i-gel insertion. What should be done?
options: Perform a jaw thrust and insert with a deep rotation
Apply firm steady force until the resistance gives
Withdraw and select the next smaller size
Insert a finger to guide the device past the tongue
questions.explanation: Early resistance is managed with a jaw thrust and a deep rotation of the device. Excessive force is forbidden, and it is not necessary to put fingers or thumbs into the patient's mouth during insertion.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: How is i-gel placement confirmed?
options: Waveform ETCO2 plus lung sounds in both fields and the epigastrium
Chest rise together with misting in the device
Aspiration of gastric contents through the gastric channel
questions.explanation: Confirmation requires waveform ETCO2 and auscultation of both lung fields and over the epigastrium. Epigastric sounds would indicate the device is seated incorrectly and ventilating the stomach.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: In which i-gel sizes may a #10 feeding tube be passed down the gastric channel?
questions.explanation: The gastric channel will accept a #10 feeding tube only in size 1.5 and above; the size 1 neonatal device cannot take one. Decompressing the stomach reduces regurgitation risk around the cuff.

questions.title: i-gel© Supraglottic Airway
questions.stem: The taped securement technique for the i-gel applies to which sizes?
questions.explanation: The two-piece nylon tape technique exists for the small devices — sizes 1 through 2.5 — because these tubes are too small for a commercial securement device. Adult sizes are secured with a commercial device.

questions.title: Inline Nebulizer Treatment
questions.stem: Which condition is an indication for inline nebulizer treatment?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm, croup/epiglottitis/laryngospasm and hyperkalemia are the listed indications — the last because nebulized beta-agonist drives potassium intracellularly. There are no listed contraindications.

questions.title: Inline Nebulizer Treatment
questions.stem: In the adult/pediatric ventilator circuit, where does the inline nebulizer set-up sit?
options: Between the flow sensor and the vent tubing
Between the ETT and the ETCO2 adaptor
Between the ETCO2 adaptor and the flow sensor
Between the ETT and the flow sensor
questions.explanation: The circuit runs ETT > ETCO2 > flow sensor > inline neb set-up > vent tubing. Placing the nebulizer distal to the flow sensor would add dead space and corrupt the measured volumes.

questions.title: Inline Nebulizer Treatment
questions.stem: What results from connecting an inline nebulizer between the flow sensor and the ETT?
options: Increased dead space and incorrect measurements
Delivery of the drug into the expiratory limb
questions.explanation: Putting the nebulizer distal to the flow sensor adds dead space between the sensor and the patient and makes the ventilator's measurements wrong. This is the single most common inline nebulizer set-up error.

questions.title: Inline Nebulizer Treatment
questions.stem: During an inline nebulizer treatment on the Hamilton T1, for how long is the fixed nebulizer flow synchronized with the inspiratory phase of each breath?
questions.explanation: The Hamilton T1 runs the fixed nebulizer flow, using 100% O2, synchronized to inspiration for 30 minutes. Crews should expect the feature to stop on its own at that point rather than when the medication cup empties.

questions.title: Inline Nebulizer Treatment
questions.stem: For an inline nebulizer treatment on the Hamilton T1, a pneumatic nebulizer connected to the nebulizer port is optimally specified for approximately what flow?
questions.explanation: The Hamilton T1 nebulizer port is specified for roughly 8 L/min, and the ventilator automatically compensates for the added volume so the set tidal volume is still delivered. The 6 L/min figure is the LTV/ReVel drive port flow.

questions.title: Inline Nebulizer Treatment
questions.stem: When an inline nebulizer is activated on the LTV/ReVel ventilator, what nominal flow is delivered to the nebulizer drive port?
questions.explanation: The LTV/ReVel delivers a six L/min nominal flow of 100% oxygen to the nebulizer drive port, and reduces inspiratory limb flow to compensate at the patient wye. The 8 L/min figure belongs to the Hamilton T1.

questions.title: Inline Nebulizer Treatment
questions.stem: How is an Aerogen nebulizer connected to the Hamilton T1 for an inline nebulizer treatment?
options: Via the USB port on the side of the ventilator
Via the nebulizer port on the front panel
Via a T piece in the inspiratory limb
questions.explanation: The Aerogen is a vibrating-mesh device and takes its power from the USB port on the side of the Hamilton T1, not from the pneumatic nebulizer port used by jet nebulizers.

questions.title: Intracranial Pressure Monitoring
questions.stem: Which finding is an indication for intracranial pressure monitoring?
questions.explanation: Intraventricular bleeds, CT showing edema and/or shifts, confirmed head injury with GCS < 8 and posturing are the indications. There are no listed contraindications.

questions.title: Intracranial Pressure Monitoring
questions.stem: Below which Glasgow Coma Scale score is ICP monitoring indicated for a confirmed head injury?
questions.explanation: A confirmed head injury with a GCS below 8 is a listed indication, matching the conventional threshold at which a patient can no longer protect the airway or be followed by serial neuro exam.

questions.title: Intracranial Pressure Monitoring
questions.stem: Level with which anatomic landmark is the ICP transducer placed and secured?
questions.explanation: The transducer is leveled to the foramen of Monro, on the same side the ventriculostomy catheter is inserted. A transducer leveled anywhere else produces an ICP reading that is wrong by the height difference.

questions.title: Intracranial Pressure Monitoring
questions.stem: With what is the ICP transducer system primed?
options: Normal saline under a pressure bag
questions.explanation: Priming uses preservative-free normal saline under strict aseptic technique. IV fluids must not be hung and a pressure bag must not be used — any pressurized infusion into a ventriculostomy is dangerous.

questions.title: Intracranial Pressure Monitoring
questions.stem: During ICP monitoring, what is the first step in zeroing the ventriculostomy line?
options: Turn the stopcock open to air
Replace the cap and close the stopcock to air
questions.explanation: The stopcock is opened to air first, the waveform is observed to flatten, Zero is pressed, and only then is the cap replaced and the stopcock closed to air to begin transducing. Pressing Zero before opening to air zeroes against the patient's pressure.

questions.title: Intracranial Pressure Monitoring
questions.stem: During ICP monitoring, when must the ventriculostomy drain be closed during transport?
options: For all patient movements and altitude changes
Only when the ICP exceeds the ordered threshold
questions.explanation: The drain is closed for every patient movement and every altitude change. An open drain during a position or pressure change can siphon CSF uncontrollably.

questions.title: Intracranial Pressure Monitoring
questions.stem: What is required each time the aircraft changes altitude with an ICP monitor in place?
options: Re-level the transducer to the foramen of Monro
Open the drain to equalize the pressure
questions.explanation: The transducer must be zeroed with each altitude change, because the reference pressure the system was zeroed against has moved. The drain stays closed throughout the altitude change.

questions.title: Intranasal Medication Delivery
questions.stem: What is the indication for intranasal medication delivery?
options: IV access is not present or is undesirable
The patient is combative and cannot be restrained
The patient has a documented allergy to IM medications
Rapid onset is required during cardiac arrest
questions.explanation: The intranasal route exists for when IV access is absent or undesirable — the classic cases being a seizing patient, a combative overdose, or a child in whom a line would delay treatment.

questions.title: Intranasal Medication Delivery
questions.stem: Which finding contraindicates intranasal medication delivery?
questions.explanation: Facial trauma, epistaxis, nasal congestion or discharge, and recent nasal cocaine use are the contraindications — each either blocks the mucosa or washes the drug away before it can be absorbed.

questions.title: Intranasal Medication Delivery
questions.stem: For intranasal medication delivery in a patient aged 10 years or older, what is the maximum volume per nostril?
questions.explanation: Patients 10 years and older take no more than 1 mL per nostril. Larger volumes run out of the nose or down the pharynx instead of being absorbed across the nasal mucosa.

questions.title: Intranasal Medication Delivery
questions.stem: For intranasal medication delivery in a child under 10 years of age, what is the maximum volume per nostril?
questions.explanation: Children under 10 take no more than 0.5 mL per nostril — half the adult limit. If the calculated volume exceeds this, the concentration must be increased rather than the volume.

questions.title: Intranasal Medication Delivery
questions.stem: For intranasal medication delivery, how much extra medication is drawn into the syringe to account for atomizer dead space?
questions.explanation: An extra 0.1 mL is drawn up because that volume remains in the mucosal atomizer device and never reaches the patient. Omitting it under-doses every intranasal administration.

questions.title: Intranasal Medication Delivery
questions.stem: During intranasal medication delivery, once the MAD is inserted into the nares, toward what is the tip aimed?
options: The top of the ipsilateral ear
questions.explanation: Aiming at the top of the ear on the same side directs the spray onto the highly vascular superior turbinate region. Aiming at the septum sprays the drug onto a poorly absorbing surface.

questions.title: Intranasal Medication Delivery
questions.stem: During intranasal medication delivery, when is the plunger depressed?
options: Slowly at the start of inhalation
Rapidly at the peak of inhalation
questions.explanation: The plunger is pushed rapidly, timed to exhalation but before the next breath in, so the atomized drug is deposited on the mucosa rather than inhaled into the lower airway.

questions.title: Intranasal Medication Delivery
questions.stem: What portion of the total intranasal dose is given in each nare?
options: Half of the total dose in each nare
The entire dose in the larger nare
The entire dose divided over three doses
questions.explanation: Half the total dose goes in each nostril, doubling the mucosal surface area available for absorption and keeping the per-nostril volume within the 1 mL (or 0.5 mL pediatric) limit.

questions.title: Intranasal Medication Delivery
questions.stem: To improve the success of intranasal medication delivery, what is the guidance on drug volume and concentration?
options: Minimize the volume and maximize the concentration
Maximize the volume and dilute the drug
Match the volume to the patient's weight
Use the standard IV concentration unchanged
questions.explanation: Absorption is limited by mucosal surface area, not by volume, so the smallest possible volume of the most concentrated preparation works best. Extra diluent simply runs out of the nose.
